title: Trump Sets the Olive Branch on Fire
text:
P resident Trump made a brief nod toward bipartisanship after his party’s historic losses in the midterms. It was very brief. You probably missed it.

 Trump did say on Election Night that he’d be willing to work with Democrats, but as he watched television in the days that followed and called his outside advisers, he grew steadily angrier. He had been on the campaign trail for weeks and had spent more than $300 million—but believed he got nothing for it, one of those advisers and a White House official familiar with the president’s complaints told me. Trump needed someone to blame; he needed to reconnect with his base; and he needed to ward off the investigations that Democrats were promising to launch.

 So Trump, as he often does when facing a political crisis, shifted into combat mode. He elevated a hard-liner to be White House chief of staff and welcomed another to become the new leader of the House Republicans. He questioned the validity of election results. He called for corruption probes into (only) blue states and cities. And then he suggested that any Democrat who tried to investigate his administration could find themselves in jail. He called them “Dumocrats.” The olive branch had been set alight.

 Democrats, still giddy over the huge margins they will soon have in both the House and the Senate, are attempting to find their own strategy. The party’s big wins mean members with a lot of different agendas will be sworn in to Congress in early January; divisions are emerging over just how aggressively they should wield their new oversight powers—and if doing so will distract from fulfilling their campaign promises to focus on affordability issues. Already there are signs of internal strife ahead of what could be contentious leadership elections.

 In the new year, Democrats and Republicans will face off along Pennsylvania Avenue as Congress battles the administration. But before that happens, Democrats have their own internal fights to resolve.

 T o the surprise of many around Trump, the president seemed somewhat blasé ahead of the election as he barnstormed the country in support of Republican candidates, two longtime outside advisers told me on the condition of anonymity to discuss private conversations. Sure, Trump wanted the GOP to win. But he seemed more obsessed with his plans to remodel Washington, and the appearances of handsome men—fixations that came at the expense of talking about the economy. The president believed that Republicans would outperform the polls again, but he was comfortable with the idea of Democrats taking control of the House and giving him a useful foil.

 What he did not expect was a wipeout. Democrats have now captured at least 55 Senate seats and at least 256 House seats. The party won in places that would have been inconceivable a year ago: Texas , Ohio, Iowa, South Carolina, and, stunningly, Mississippi. (Mississippi!) On Election Night, Trump, sounding almost shell-shocked, told The New York Times in a phone call that he would honor the results and would “look forward to working” with the Democrats. He tried to distance himself from the loss by insisting that his name had not been on the ballot, even though he had repeatedly asked voters to pretend that it was.

 In the days that followed, the graciousness faded as Trump’s anger built, and he shifted back to his more comfortable setting. The president pushed out Susie Wiles, his chief of staff, who was well liked internally, and who had overseen the ruthless rollout of his agenda and efforts to expand executive power. Wiles, at times, tried to steer Trump away from some of his most extreme impulses; her successor, Stephen Miller, seems certain to do no such thing. Miller is the architect of the administration’s mass-deportation program—deemed too extreme by many voters and “too tough” by the president himself. Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader who is expected to become speaker, flatly said “no” when asked last week whether he could work with Miller, whom he then declared “a stone-cold racist” and “reckless extremist.” Miller has signaled to administration officials that the deportation program will expand and that he wants to make the most of Trump’s last two years in power, the White House official told me, speaking on the condition of anonymity to share internal discussions. There is no sign of moderation.

 That’s not the only place where the president is doubling down on things that voters just rejected. Americans dislike the interminable Iran war—and the resulting oil-price hikes. Even some Republicans have quietly expressed a willingness to make Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth the fall guy for both. Trump spent weeks querying outside advisers for their views on Hegseth but had not committed to making a change. The defense secretary’s job security got a boost when Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a Republican whom Trump loathes, moved with Democrats to impeach Hegseth. The secretary held a defiant news conference last week and made his case to an Audience of One that he should keep his post. It worked: Trump posted his support for Hegseth, and Republicans voted down the impeachment. Hegseth will face a further judgment once Democrats take power next year, but Trump saw the vote as a sign that he still controls the party that he led to defeat.

 [ Read: Repudiation ] 

 Nearly all Republican lawmakers in swing districts lost their races, which means the next GOP caucus will be filled with MAGA true believers—those whose districts are so conservative that they require moving far to the right to get through a primary. They picked Jim Jordan, an uncompromising hard-liner, as their new minority leader.

 Trump has also tried to short-circuit impending Democratic-led investigations . In his first term, his administration largely refused to comply with congressional subpoenas, a tactic likely to be repeated, the White House official told me. But now Trump has raised the stakes. The White House’s top lawyer has threatened Democrats in Congress that efforts to probe the administration could be criminal, an assertion that would likely be tossed out by the courts. Trump on Thursday went on a Truth Social posting spree to assert, without evidence, that there was widespread corruption in blue states and Democratic-run cities, despite polls that have suggested that Americans are deeply fed up with his administration’s alleged graft.

 Trump’s attention simply seems off. On Friday, a ground stop brought air travel across the country to a halt, sparking initial fears of cyberterrorism and leaving tens of thousands of passengers stranded. With the airports in chaos, Trump huddled in the Oval Office with Jon Voight, the actor, two people familiar with the meeting told me on the condition of anonymity to discuss private conversations. Trump then called a series of Hollywood power players to discuss legislation to revitalize the entertainment industry—prompting one to ask if his focus would be better spent on the air-travel emergency.

 Trump demurred. He posted on social media later that day about the show-business bill. He didn’t address the FAA meltdown until yesterday.

 T he breadth of Democratic wins this month—and their decisive margins—has injected a renewed energy into a party that, two years ago, seemed on life support. Though most in the party recognize that the election was more of a rejection of Trump than an endorsement of Democrats, the sense of giddiness is palpable. They won, and they won big. But to invoke Robert Redford’s character at the end of The Candidate : “What do we do now?”

 Democrats are, well, Democrats, so a fear is already settling in that somehow they’ll blow this. Some of their first steps have not been great: 11 Democrats missed the Hegseth vote (many claimed that they were stuck in traffic) and some infighting has erupted about picking leaders. The left has accused both Jeffries and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of being insufficiently aggressive in their opposition to Trump and overly supportive of Israel in its war in Gaza. Jeffries seems all but certain to secure the top post in the House; he would be the first Black speaker, and few in the party seem prepared to block that history, particularly after inspirational victories by Black candidates in places such as Georgia and Mississippi.

 [ Read: The simple message that produced a Democratic landslide ] 

 Schumer, Democrats tell me, may have a more complicated path to remaining on top of the Senate caucus. He served ably in the role during President Biden’s four years in office—particularly the first two, when he navigated a slim majority to steer through major legislation. But he drew criticism from within the party once Trump came back to power last year, particularly over a deal to avoid a government shutdown. The 75-year-old is also too old for those who want generational change, and he is the latest example of how support for Israel is shaping up to be a Democratic litmus test ; though Schumer has turned on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, progressives believe he was too slow to get tough with the Israeli leader.

 This year’s Democratic victories should help Schumer’s case. He had a few missteps in picking Senate candidates (his initial choices lost primaries in Maine and Michigan), and was perceived as slow to help some nominees in the South. But he also recruited an impressive string of unexpected winners, including in Iowa and Ohio. And, as one of his allies succinctly put it to me, he can “point to the scoreboard” and take credit for many of the at least 55 Democratic seats. That hasn’t been enough, however, to deter his challenger for the party’s leadership: Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland.

 Most Democrats think Schumer will be selected as leader again. There is wisdom, his advocates believe, in having a Washington veteran in charge, especially because several Democratic senators will likely be tied up with 2028 presidential campaigns. It’s not clear whether Schumer himself will be running for office that year. Announcing that he will not seek reelection, some allies theorize, might make it easier to secure the full support of his conference, allowing his skeptics to rationalize the choice as a temporary, caretaker role—and opening a wide path for Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to fill his New York seat if she opts to run for the Senate instead of the White House.

 N o matter which Democrats end up leading the two chambers, they will have numbers on their side: The party’s margins are so big that each leader will be able to pass legislation while ignoring the demands of certain factions (such as, perhaps, the Democratic Socialists of America). The landslide will also allow lawmakers, especially those from swing districts or red states, to vote “no” on bills that are unpopular back home without endangering the legislation’s chances of passing. But there are debates in the party as to what legislation to pass first: Something on affordability? A health-care fix? Ethics reform? Curtailing ICE?

 Most Democrats I have spoken with since Election Day believe that they should focus on the economic issues that got them elected and send a series of bills to Trump’s desk, daring him to veto them. If Trump signs, then it’s a bipartisan win and, hopefully, the American people would also benefit (the president in a recent interview said he would consider “reasonable” ideas from Democrats but stayed light on specifics). If he refuses, then, yes, voters might unleash their anger on both parties. But Democrats largely think that Trump, who is already unpopular, would take most of the blame—and that they could tie Trump’s decision to any Republican who might run in 2028, particularly Vice President Vance.

 Democrats know that they also need to hold the Trump administration accountable. Party leaders have waved off talk of impeaching the president for a third time; it could backfire, allowing Trump to play the victim and even boosting his approval ratings, as happened in 2019. But there are other avenues, including impeaching Cabinet members and opening up probes into the business dealings of staffers and their families. One name mentioned to me by several Democrats: Jared Kushner, who has acted as an unofficial secretary of state while also doing business around the globe. Many in the party believe that the election results reflect anger that people in Trump’s universe have profited while average Americans struggle. But there are so many allegations of corruption, Democrats have said, that investigating all of them could seem like overreach. One Democratic strategist told me that an option being considered is to focus on a few easy-to-understand stories that would tell the bigger picture: the Qatari-gifted Air Force One, for example.

 [ Read: The Qataris gave Trump an airplane. He crippled their country in return. ] 

 Trump is weighing some counterpunches. Staring down investigations, irrelevancy, and a possible Democratic successor’s Department of Justice, no one expects him to go quietly. He still has broad powers, particularly in foreign affairs, and is poised for a fight. But in the two weeks since his electoral comeuppance, he has appeared unsure. His claims of election fraud seem half-hearted. He reheated another warning about a mysterious caravan of migrants coming up from Mexico. His vice president publicly broke with him on the Iran war.

 Trump admitted earlier this month that his White House was “having a very bad press day,” so he jokingly suggested that UFC head Dana White take over as press secretary to create a distraction. He even paraded White at a news conference to keep it going. But nearly all of the questions were about the election losses—and the challenges ahead for a diminished president.
